stories.headline: MAPS: Netflix’s Multimodal Asset Personalization at Scale
stories.summary: By Emma Yanyang Kong , Aditya Deshpande , Asad Abbasi , Bowei Yan , David Fagnan , Ashish Rastogi , Dhaval Patel , Ray Zhang Introduction The Netflix experience is a journey of discovery. Every visual cue, from the artwork on a title to the video previews that autoplay while you browse, is there to connect you with a story you will love.
stories.why_it_matters: We call these visual cues assets , and choosing the right one for each member is a personalization problem of its own. This marks a notable development for engineering teams working in big tech.
key_points: Problem & Context: But which image or video preview of Squid Game should we show you? And what do we do right after a title launches, when there’s far too little interaction data to know which asset we should recommend to each member? For years, our models answered the first question well and the second poorly.

Technical Implementation: Right after a title launched, its assets had no history, so we dialed up exploration on its assets to gather interaction data, and otherwise fell back to popularity heuristics that ignore your taste.
Deployment & Impact: This post shares how multimodal embeddings let our models see and hear the assets they recommend, so personalization can kick in far sooner, close to a title’s launch.

stories.headline: Automatic Key Exchange: faster, post-quantum secure origin handshakes for 45 billion daily connections (and counting)
stories.summary: Every time Cloudflare opens a new TLS 1.3 connection to an origin server, we have to make a guess: the protocol requires us to commit to a key agreement algorithm in the very first packet we send, before the origin has told us anything about itself or what it can support. If we guess right, the handshake completes in one round trip.
stories.why_it_matters: Guess wrong, and the origin replies with a HelloRetryRequest , we start over, and the connection costs two round trips. This marks a notable development for engineering teams working in cloud.
key_points: Problem & Context: Every time Cloudflare opens a new TLS 1.3 connection to an origin server, we have to make a guess: the protocol requires us to commit to a key agreement algorithm in the very first packet we send, before the origin has told us anything about itself or what it can support.
Technical Implementation: Widely supported, but as it turns out, suboptimal for roughly 30% of the origin connections we've since measured.

Deployment & Impact: We probe each origin to learn which key agreement algorithms it supports and prefers, then lead with that algorithm on the first try, preferring the post-quantum hybrid X25519MLKEM768 wherever the origin can speak it.
